articles.title: Philippine diplomats joined walkout on Netanyahu at UN, DFA confirms
articles.summary: The Philippines was among delegates who walked out of the United Nations General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech on Friday, September 25, according to the…

blocks.text: September 27, 2026 | 3:12pm
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, on September 24, 2026.
AFP / Timothy Clary

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines was among delegates who walked out of the United Nations General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech on Thursday, September 24, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Clips of the session show dozens of delegates leaving their seats in protest and streaming toward the exits just as Netanyahu stood at the podium to deliver his address.
Other delegates stayed seated and some stood to applaud him amid repeated calls for order.

The available footage does not clearly show where the Philippine delegation was. With no official roll call, tallies compiled by news outlets and observers drew on video and photos of the hall, and some placed the Philippines among the delegations that stayed.

"The Philippines joined the walk out in global solidarity for peace in the Middle East and the call for all parties to desist from unilateral actions that erode the conditions of peace," DFA Spokesperson Analyn Ratonel told Philstar.com in a message.
The DFA spokesperson said such actions undermine the viability of a future Palestinian state.

"The Philippines is deeply concerned about the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and notes with alarm Israel's efforts to advance the E1 settlement plan, and the continued rise of settler violence in the West Bank," the DFA spokesperson said.
"These actions are detrimental to finding a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the Middle East conflict," she added.
The Philippines "has always supported the two-state solution as the viable path to peace in the region," the DFA spokesperson said.
Before the speech by the Israeli leader, the Palestinian Mission to the UN had urged member states to fill the hall with staff and leave together once Netanyahu was introduced, according to reports.
The mission urged member states to show their objection to what it described as Israel's genocide, war crimes and illegal occupation.
Netanyahu, who visibly paused before he began his speech, reacted to the throngs of delegates leaving the hall by inviting "any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall" to go.
The Israeli leader's UN General Assembly speeches also drew walkouts in 2024 and 2025.
A week before Netanyahu's UN address, the DFA issued a similar statement protesting Israel's E1 settlement plan on September 17.
In that statement, the department said Israel's push to advance the E1 plan and the rise in settler violence "may contravene international law."
It also said Manila would continue to uphold the Palestinian people's right to self-determination.

articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Sunday questioned the Department of Public Works and Highways over a supposed project in Taguig City whose coordinates were located in the Visayas based on geotagged photos.

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 3:02pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Sunday questioned the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) over a supposed project in Taguig City whose coordinates were located in the Visayas based on geotagged photos.

“Sec. Vince Dizon, please explain how this finding of your own team should not be flagged as a ghost project in Taguig. (Since when has Taguig been located in Leyte?)” he said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
The senator cited that the geotagged photos of the projects attached to the billing reports “reflected coordinates located approximately 600 kilometers away in Leyte Province.”
Lacson also claimed that the said project’s contractor is linked to the Discaya couple, who are big figures in the flood control scandal.
“To further highlight the red flag, Discaya’s St Timothy ang contractor. What do you say about this, Sec?” he said in a separate X post.
The senator’s social media post came after DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said that his office has yet to find a ghost or non-existent infrastructure project in Taguig City.
Meanwhile, DPWH Undersecretary Ricardo Bernabe III also claimed that their agency has so far listed 107 projects in Taguig, all of which have accomplishments.
In another X post, Lacson said that Dizon was suffering from a “clouded” memory following the DPWH chief’s claims about Taguig infrastructures.

"Poor DPWH Site Inspection Engineers. Their boss, Sec. Vince Dizon directly contradicted their own site inspection reports in Taguig, specifically submitted by personnel from the department's Bureau of Quality and Safety and Bureau of Maintenance," Lacson said in a post.
GMA News Online has reached out to Dizon for comment but he has yet to issue a statement as of posting time. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Asian Games organizer says sorry for logistical headaches
articles.summary: The unexpected surge of late entries has strained accommodation and transport networks in the Asian Games, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and…

blocks.text: STAY. A man walks near Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which will serve as a floating temporary athletes' village for 4,000 to 5,000 participants during the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games, after it docked at the port of Nagoya, Japan, September 15, 2026.
Edgar SuREUTERS

The unexpected surge of late entries has strained accommodation and transport networks in the Asian Games, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and travel delays

NAGOYA, Japan – The chief organizer of the Asian Games apologized on Saturday, September 26, for the logistical headaches plaguing the event, saying a late influx of athletes and officials had made it difficult to extend smooth service.

The number of participants at the continental showpiece ballooned to 17,000 following a flurry of late entries — around 2,000 more than the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games Organising Committee had initially projected.
The unexpected surge strained accommodation and transport networks, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and travel delays.
“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport, for various reasons,” AINAGOC Secretary General Satoshi Murate told a press conference.
“Whatever the cause, AINAGOC is responsible for providing the service, and I frankly apologzse for the mistakes.

“Our staff work every day to identify the causes of each mistake and make sure they don’t happen again. I think you can see that accommodation and transport have improved greatly compared with the early days.”
Murate added that maintaining consistent service standards had proved challenging following the “significant” increase in delegation sizes.
“Our top priority is making sure the athletes can compete at their best. We are fully committed to making the necessary improvements to ensure that they can do so,” he said.

“We are already working on a number of improvements, and in the second half of the Games, we want to make sure those efforts produce results and that we can manage things more smoothly and effectively.”
Mongolian women’s basketball coach Javier Garcia Alvarez criticized the transport system after a training session had to be scrapped when the team bus failed to arrive.
“I played in many FIBA Asia basketball cups and even Asian Games in Incheon some years ago. I never had this kind of issue that the bus is not coming for practice,” he told Reuters.
“It was kind of disappointing because we were planning some practice, some shooting for the girls and the mind was prepared for that, and then at the end we had to cancel.”
Filipino squash player Yvonne Alyssa Dalida had to endure a lengthy wait before checking into her room aboard a chartered cruise ship, though she found a silver lining in the unconventional setup.
“I think Japan or AINAGOC could have prepared better for this event, but I find it cool as well because it’s very unique.”
“I’ve never been on a cruise, so I think that’s also the upside of them using this.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘It’s like the Scottish Upper East Side’: shame and snobbery as American students blamed for St Andrews classism
articles.summary:
Online comments reflect class tensions at Scottish university between those from lower-income families and wealthier US undergraduates

When Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return…

blocks.text: When Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return to St Andrews University this academic year because of her experiences of classism on campus, she did not expect much of a response. But in the two weeks since she published her story on LinkedIn, it has resonated with hundreds of others.

“Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” the former comparative literature and classical studies student wrote in a lengthy post. “Arriving at a university ranked first in the UK at the time from a background like mine, I thought I was doing everything right.

“I don’t mean for this to be a sob story but an explanation. I recognise the privilege of access to higher education, however I am also brutally aware of the hidden privilege of having unobstructed access to studying for a degree. There is a deep gap between the two, and it is never addressed.”

For many responding, her comments touched on a growing tension at St Andrews, driven by the funding model of Scotland’s cash-strapped universities. Places for Scottish students, who study for free, are capped by the Scottish government and account for about 30% of students at St Andrews. Maintenance loans and bursaries cover basic costs, but those from lower-income families are still often left with less disposable income than their contemporaries – including wealthy international students who pay much higher fees.

St Andrews, ranked second in the Guardian’s university league table for 2026, accepts one of the highest percentages in the UK of privately educated students. The British aristocracy has long adored the medieval town’s cobbled streets, wind-swept beach and grand stone buildings: Prince William and the Princess of Wales met there.

blocks.caption: Sophie Rose Jenkins’ comments have struck a chord with some other students. Photograph: none

blocks.text: But the recent influx of wealthy US students has changed the dynamic on campus, students say. Americans account for around a fifth of undergraduates at St Andrews, the highest proportion in the UK, with each paying £33,250 for this academic year, more than three times what British students pay.

“My parents were worried about me coming here. They didn’t want me to be left out,” said one Scottish fresher who is on a scholarship to study classics. “Most of the people I have met are international students. I didn’t grow up with tons of money. Maybe they can be a bit ignorant to the cost of things.”
Another said: “There’s a Pret here. You have to ask yourself why that is in such a small town.”

Aspects of fraternity and sorority culture have started to blend with the upper-class experience of British university, some students say. Regular black-tie dinners and balls are now rivalled by fashion shows and exclusive societies. A short walk from the student union bar, an interior design shop advertises luxury bed linen for students, while a popular coffee shop sells designer clothes and candles alongside speciality matchas.

“I totally see her [Jenkins’s] perspective,” said one privately educated student from Edinburgh, who was returning from hockey practice with friends. “It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans. We knew lots of people from hockey already so it’s easy to feel left out if you’re not from that environment.

“The American culture is coming in and it massively influences everything at the moment. They compete with each other. If you look at how they dress, people arrive in lectures as if they are going on a night out.”

One student referenced a well-known student newspaper article published last year about how St Andrews had turned into the Scottish Upper East Side, which said: “Our beloved Scottish town is day by day turning into a microcosm of Manhattan’s elite world; complete with intrigue, privilege, and secrets that spread like wildfire.”

Underlining the point, an American student walks past the student union loudly explaining to a friend: “Everyone is going to think you’re rich if you have a Ralph Lauren bag. But that doesn’t make you rich.”

St Andrews said it had reached out to Jenkins to better understand her experience, but she had decided not to engage for now. It said it had a robust system for reporting complaints from students, and only a handful of complaints had been made in the last five years.

“Yes, some students do arrive here in St Andrews, and at every other university, with immature, offensive and classist views. But they tend not to leave with them,” said the vice-principal Niall Scott.

“This isn’t a St Andrews issue – it’s a societal issue. Classism begins in the home or at school, not at university. Universities like St Andrews have a crucial role to play in challenging these attitudes by bringing together people from different backgrounds, cultures and perspectives, encouraging understanding, respect and inclusion.”

The debate around classism at Scottish universities is not new. In 2024, Edinburgh University offered guidance on how students should treat one another after rising claims of discrimination and classism. “Don’t be a snob!” read the advice given out to students. At St Andrews, some students said the issue of classism was not only linked to the rise in American students.

“It is generally an attitude thing. There is an idea that working-class students can’t speak about issues that are going on elsewhere in the world because they are not as well travelled,” said one science student. “At St Andrews, even for moderately wealthy people, it feels like there is an old money level above that you don’t even get to speak to.”
Rasmus, a Danish student, said he was bemused by the social dynamics at the university.

“It took two weeks for me to meet a Scottish person. They are surrounded by people here who have the money for international tuition, which is quite narrow. I can imagine that being quite a difficult experience,” he said.

articles.title: [Tech Thoughts] How bad actors weaponize copyright to silence journalism online
articles.summary: Bad actors use legitimate takedown mechanisms to remove journalistic content they don't want online

blocks.text: Bad actors use legitimate takedown mechanisms to remove journalistic content they don't want online

items: The author learns about how bad actors exploit copyright and social media moderation to silence investigative journalism.
These bad actors use tactics such as cloning content, backdating it, and making false reports to social media companies to remove legitimate journalistic work.
To combat this issue, journalists can seek help from organizations like Access Now and advocate for accountability from social media platforms regarding their takedown processes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

As a journalist whose primary world is being online, I didn’t really think much about how social media impacted the reach of stories. My concerns were mostly about writing stories, leaving much of the amplification of my work to others in Rappler.

It wasn’t until I attended an online webinar this week that I learned more about how bad actors use copyright and weaponize social media moderation and website takedown mechanisms to silence journalists and weaken — or negate — the reach of investigative journalism.
The webinar, hosted by the Global Investigative Journalist Network (GIJN), had experts speaking out about instances journalists from around the world had experienced being silenced.
This isn’t a physical access issue, like what would happen if a president barred a reporter or a group of reporters within a press pool from being able to be in the same room with the president.

Instead, the webinar shared experiences and case studies showing how rampant and far-reaching the effects of bad actors are when they undertake the process of copyright-striking legitimate pages to get them taken down or to otherwise negate the ability of an investigative journalism piece to be shared or read.

There are a number of ways in which this takes shape, but in broad strokes, it’s basically stealing and backdating content or faking evidence to make it appear as if the bad actors are the originators of the content seeking to be taken down.

There is apparently a thriving industry of “reputation management groups,” whether legitimate businesses or just smaller unofficial outfits willing to do dirty work for money, that advertise specific services. like content removal, webpage removal, mass reporting, astroturfing, or similar tasks.

To silence journalists, these bad actors make false reports to social media companies and fake evidence against legitimate groups or posts to get the social media companies’ automated systems to do the work of taking down a page for them.
For instance, Bangladeshi-based networks were operating to take down content in Central Asia and Africa.

To get takedowns done on social media, they would clone videos or steal the text of reports — say from an African investigative report. The bad actors would then, in the case of videos, add Bengali voiceovers on top of videos to make it seem from their region.

For videos or text pieces, they would then falsify further by backdating the content on social media or on a legitimate-seeming website so that they could say the content came from them and request the takedown of posts from the automated systems handling moderation on social media platforms like Facebook or X.

In some other instances, bad actors abuse the memorialization feature of Facebook — the feature that creates a static memorial page for dead Facebook users — to disable the posting capabiltiies of specific journalists.

The memorialization trick is more involved, as it requires falsifying death certificates and submitting the fake death certificate and possibly other documents to Facebook so the page can be memorialized.
In other parts of the world, where investigative journalists or teams work together and have a website for their investigations, copyright abuse is the trick used to get legitimate sites taken down.
Similar to social media takedowns, copyright abuse see bad actors cloning content and making a false website that backdates the content.

They then make bogus copyright requests so legitimate sites can be taken down and their search results scrubbed from search engines through the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act, even if the sites aren’t based in the United States.
While journalists are fighting the good fight of doing research and investigating anomalies, there are ways in which things could change to make this industry die out.

For victims of such actions, they can reach out to Access Now, a global nonprofit organization that helps get people back online by defending digital rights, or seek help from their local digital rights helpline, if a country has one.

Journalists may also want to investigate these malign actors, while digital advocacy groups can hold platforms — especially social media platforms frightened by intellectual property claims — accountable for offloading takedown requests to machines rather than humans. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Chinese Embassy slams US for backing PH in Ayungin
articles.summary: The Chinese Embassy on Sunday hit back at the US Embassy after the latter sided with the Philippines over Beijing's reported interference in Manila's recent rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 2:56pm

The Chinese Embassy on Sunday hit back at the US Embassy after the latter sided with the Philippines over Beijing's reported interference in Manila's recent rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal.

“We strongly condemn the US Embassy in the Philippines’ disregard for right and wrong and its insistence on supporting the Philippines’ provocative and unlawful actions at Ren’ai Reef in China’s Nansha Qundao,” the Chinese Embassy said in a statement.

China issued the statement hours after US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton described the maneuvers by the China Coast Guard (CCG) and the People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) as “dangerous” and “irresponsible.”
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) earlier said three PLAN warships and five CCG vessels, including two Houbei-class missile boats, interfered with the mission.
The AFP said the Philippine RoRe mission was temporarily suspended due to the possibility of escalation that could endanger personnel and vessels.
However, the Chinese Embassy maintained that the Philippines had “breached its commitments” while disregarding China's warnings.

“The Philippines’ provocative actions and its subsequent hype and publicity during a traditional Chinese festival seriously violated the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) and severely undermined peace and stability in the South China Sea region,” it said.
The US Embassy, for its part, called on China to stop its provocations.

“We stand by our Philippine Allies and laud their professionalism and restraint. We call on the China Coast Guard and PLAN to cease the use of escalatory tactics that threaten the freedom of navigation and a free and open Indo-Pacific,” said Lipton.
China, however, told the US “to stop fanning the flames and refrain from actions that undermine regional peace and stability.”
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled on a case brought by the Philippines challenging China's maritime claims in the South China Sea.

Among its findings, the tribunal said there was no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources within the sea areas falling within its nine-dash line. China has rejected the ruling and does not recognize it.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-cop who claimed cash deliveries to Sara Duterte dismissed from PNP
articles.summary: Under a dismissal order dated September 15, Rodulfo Gracioso was dismissed from police service on Sept. 11, 2026.

blocks.text: September 27, 2026 | 2:44pm

Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte speaks during a press conference at her office in Manila on December 11, 2024. Philippine lawmakers on February 5 voted to send articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte to the Senate, a day before the current congressional session was set to end.
AFP / Ted Aljibe
MANILA, Philippines — The former police officer who claimed to have delivered suitcases filled with massive amounts of cash to Vice President Sara Duterte has been dismissed from the police force.
Under a dismissal order dated September 15, Rodulfo Gracioso was dismissed from the police service on Sept. 11, 2026.
The dismissal order mentions three counts of grave misconduct against him.
His dismissal also carried the accessory penalties of cancellation of his eligibility, forfeiture of retirement benefits, and disqualification from re-employment in government service.
Gracioso, an ex-security aide of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco, stepped forward, claiming he helped deliver suitcases filled with large amounts of cash.
He alleged making more than 20 deliveries of cash-filled suitcases totaling more than P2 billion to Vice President Sara Duterte and over P1 billion to detained former President Rodrigo Duterte.
The vice president denied his claims, saying that she never met Gracioso.
National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag said the agency subjected Gracioso to a polygraph test and was able to validate some of his statements through other means.

Meanwhile, lawyer Rowell Ilagan dismissed Gracioso’s claims of alleged unlawful acts by Velasco and his wife, calling the claims fabricated, logically inconsistent, and contradicted by verifiable facts.

“The former Speaker of the House's record of service in the government is untainted with corruption and his wife's benevolence is widely known, leaving no basis for the illegal allegations now being suggested,” Ilagan said.
“We respectfully urge everyone to be more circumspect in appreciating this news report while we evaluate and determine the accountability of the individual and the publisher under the law,” he added.

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The United States (US) condemned China’s interference in a Philippine humanitarian rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission at Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea earlier this…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The United States (US) condemned China’s interference in a Philippine humanitarian rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission at Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea earlier this week.

In a statement Sunday, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton called out the China Coast Guard (CCG) and the People’s Liberation Army Navy’s (PLAN) “irresponsible maneuvers” that threatened a collision with a Philippine vessel and prevented a lawful and routine resupply mission to the shoal on Thursday.
“We stand by our Philippine allies and laud their professionalism and restraint,” Lipton said.
“We call on the China Coast Guard and PLAN to cease the use of escalatory tactics that threaten the freedom of navigation and a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) earlier said eight Chinese warships and coast guard vessels interfered in a Philippine Navy mission to deliver essential supplies to the Filipino crew aboard BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin.

The harassment took place from around 8:35 p.m. to 11 p.m. Thursday while the Philippine supply ship, the M/V Lapu-Lapu, along with three Philippine Navy and Coast Guard (PCG) support vessels, were approximately 60 nautical miles from Ayungin Shoal.
The Chinese side, according to the AFP, hindered the operations with continuous radio calls and monitoring, and got near the Philippine ships.
The PCG said the mission was called off at 11:08 p.m. for the safety of Philippine personnel.
The PCG’s BRP Malabrigo was deployed to “provide security assistance” during the Navy mission.

China continues to assert its ambitious claim over nearly the entire South China Sea, a claim that overlaps with the Philippines’ maritime entitlements in the West Philippine Sea under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal invalidated China’s expansive claims, ruling that its so-called “nine-dash line” has no legal basis under international law. Beijing has rejected the ruling, while Manila has repeatedly affirmed that the decision is final and binding. /mcm

articles.summary: South African police have launched a search for suspects after 17 people were found dead at a tavern southwest of Johannesburg. A separate tavern shooting near Cape Town left 10 dead.

blocks.text: At least 27 people have been killed in separate mass shooting incidents in South Africa's Gauteng and Western Cape provinces overnight.
In the first incident, gunmen armed with assault rifles killed 17 people and wounded 15 others at a bar in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg, police said on Sunday.
Manhunt underway for 8 suspects
Gauteng police said they have launched a manhunt for eight unidentified armed men following deadly shooting.
"They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles," the South African ​Police Service (SAPS) ‌said.
Emergency ‌services ‌declared all ​17 victims, 13 men and four women, dead at the scene. Authorities said the shooting occurred Saturday at around 9:30 p.m. local time (1930 UTC).
A motive for the shooting ⁠was ​not ​known, the SAPS said, adding that "suspects ​were reportedly ⁠armed with AK-47 rifles ⁠and ​pistols."
10 killed in Lwandle tavern shooting, Cape Town
In a separate shooting in the Western Cape, police said gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township at 1:46 a.m. (2346 Saturday GMT).
Authorities said five of the victims died at the scene while another five succumbed to their injuries after being taken to hospital.
Police said that no arrests have been made and that a "multi-disciplinary team" led by serious and violent crime detectives had been established to track down those responsible.
More police resources have been sent to the area as the search for the perpetrators continues.
The latest incidents came just days after at least 11 people were gunned down at a home in KwaZulu-Natal Province.
That shooting occurred in KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city.
South Africa has been grappling with violent crime and has one of the world's highest murder rates, with around 60 people dying violently in the country each day.

articles.title: London’s investment bankers and lawyers make more than £1bn in takeover frenzy
articles.summary:
Bumper fees paid in the year’s mergers and acquisitions spark anger over high City pay during cost of living crisis

London’s investment bankers and lawyers have made more than £1bn from a…

blocks.text: London’s investment bankers and lawyers have made more than £1bn from a frenzy of takeover deals this year, sparking anger over high City pay during the cost of living crisis.

The value of mergers and acquisitions of UK stock market listed companies has surged 175% in 2026 to $132.9bn (£100bn), according to the London Stock Exchange, as overseas buyers snap up British companies at record pace.
Fees paid to investment bankers, lawyers and accountants working on these deals topped £1.2bn, official filings suggest, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets.

The bumper fees were fuelled by a string of corporate takeovers driven by a flood of private equity cash and acquisitive American buyers targeting undervalued British businesses. The spree of acquisitions of listed companies has led to concerns over the future of the London stock market.

The takeover frenzy has fed advisory business at the biggest banks and law firms in the City. Bankers at JP Morgan have been the busiest, advising on more takeovers involving UK companies than any other bank this year – a total of 14 deals worth a combined $89.4bn (£67.6bn), according to the LSE. The leading law firm was Slaughter and May, it found.

UK bankers have also benefited from soaring bonuses, after the government scrapped a rule capping bonuses at two-times annual salaries in late 2023. Each bank now sets its own upward limit. Big investment banks such as Goldman Sachs now allow performers to be paid up to 25 times their annual salary.
The surge in business comes while the banking sector lobbies against paying higher taxes in the UK.

Jamie Dimon, the billionaire boss of JP Morgan, has issued several warnings to Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget on 28 October. The industry body UK Finance echoed the view this week.
Lenders in the UK currently pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets.

The most lucrative deal in the City this year was the £10.6bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by the private equity firm EQT, which is expected to generate more than £370m in fees. Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Deutsche Bank are working on the deal for EQT, while Intertek paid Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Cazenove and PJT Partners.

Lawyers at top City firms have started to out-earn some bankers. Partners at the “magic circle” firms Linklaters and Clifford Chance were paid an average of £2.5m and £2.3m respectively in the year to April, their highest ever. A&O Shearman partners were paid £2.2m.

blocks.caption: The Clifford Chance building at Canary Wharf, London. Partners at the firm were paid an average of £2.3m in the year to April.  Photograph: Robert Evans/Alamy

blocks.text: At the boutique bank Evercore, which the LSE said had advised on five deals in the UK stock market this year, the firm’s “members” – senior managing directors who are dealmakers – were paid an average of about £2m. Its best-paid member collected £16.2m this year.

Overall, dealmaker fees are likely to be even higher this year as the figures do not include deals which did not complete, were rejected or for which documents have not been published – including the £5.7bn takeover of the FTSE 100 airline easyJet by the private equity firm Apollo Global Management, agreed last month.
While pay continues to climb in the City, millions of UK households are struggling with the cost of living.
after newsletter promotion
Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the national secretary at the GMB union, said financial brokers were paid huge sums “while the people who keep this country moving struggle to make ends meet”.

“The UK needs to seriously re-examine what we value and hold dear – is it the people who build, who create, who look after us and our loved ones in their hour of need? Or is it a bloated financial sector?” she asked.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, repeated his call for a windfall tax on lenders’ profits as interest rates have risen, saying that “if banks can afford bonanza payouts for their top brass, they can clearly afford to pay more tax”.
“People up and down the country are struggling, and things could get a lot worse with energy prices set to shoot up,” he said.

Earlier this month figures from the Office for National Statistics showed that average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, slowed to 3.9% in the three months ended in July, down from 4.1% in the three months ended in June.

There are fears that, while dealmakers’ pay is rising on the takeover boom, investment banks could lose out on revenue from their sell-side research and work on flotations as more companies leave London’s stock market and fewer line up to join.

Despite hopes that 2026 could spark a revival on the UK stock market, there were just seven listings in the first half of the year, raising £577m in total, according to data from the professional services company EY. However, this week, Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, said it was planning one of the biggest UK listings in years.

articles.title: Valid visas, baseless claims: The aggressive deportation of Filipino seafarers
articles.summary: Hundreds of seafarers — mostly Filipinos — were detained at US ports and shackled for deportation following interrogations 'full of torment and terror’

blocks.text: September 27 is National Seafarers’ Day. But this year’s theme, “Marinong Filipino: Matatag sa Alon, Matibay sa Hamon!” holds special irony for Filipino seafarers caught in the US immigration crackdown known as “Operation Tidal Wave.”
Operation Tidal Wave mandates Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) to arrest and deport cruise ship workers who allegedly consume child pornography.

According to US immigration lawyer Ian Seruelo, contrary to how US immigration has operated in the past, CBP is allowed to act solely on suspicion and is not required to produce evidence to support its allegations.
This has disproportionately impacted Filipino cruise ship workers.

Approximately 278 cruise ship workers — 270 of whom are Filipinos — have been deported from US ports since April 2025. Many were longtime cruise ship workers who had experienced no issues prior to 2025.
Aqui Soriano, executive director of Pilipino Workers Center (PWC), situated these deportations within the context of a changed US immigration system.

“Now there are less guardrails,” said Aqui. “In the push to fulfill Trump’s quota of 1 million deportations, they say they are targeting criminal aliens when the vast majority have no criminal records at all.”
Deported Filipino seafarers are part of this larger trend.
On cruise ships worldwide, almost 1 out of 3 workers is Filipino.

“So is there specific targeting or is it proportional?” asks Ellene Sana, executive director of the Quezon City-based Center for Migrant Advocacy. “We don’t know. But we know the impact of the deportations is far and wide.”

Deported seafarers attest to the severe impacts. Many are the primary breadwinners for intergenerational families. Many are still in debt from the cost of trainings and certifications required to land cruise ship employment. Many of them also believe that Filipinos are being specifically targeted for deportation.

“There was one Filipino who was caught in 2024,” said Reynaldo, a deported seafarer who worked as a galley attendant. “Since then I think that’s been an excuse to randomly target other Filipinos like us.”
Seruelo agrees that deported Filipino seafarers could be the victims of collective punishment.
“This administration has the propensity to do that,” he said. “Since one or two Filipino workers have been charged, now all Filipinos are suspects.”

At a September 21st public forum in Quezon City organized by PWC, the Center for Migrant Advocacy, and the Save Our Seafarers Coalition, seafarers shared their stories of being targeted, arrested, and deported by Customs and Border Patrol. A pattern emerges from these, as well as the stories of nine other seafarers interviewed by Rappler.

The seafarers were forcibly taken from ships docked at ports throughout the US, where they were legally and diligently working as cooks, casino dealers, galley attendants, motormen, security officers, and more.

Customs and Border Patrol agents interrogated them on their ships, searched their cabins — sometimes violently — seized their phones and confiscated many of their possessions. The seafarers were then taken off the ship for further interrogation at the port, with only the uniform on their backs, then shackled and transported by third-party private drivers to the nearest airport.

At the airport, many were subjected to further interrogation for hours, in freezing temperatures with no food and little water, and were not allowed to make phone calls or even talk to their fellow detainees.

All of the deported seafarers had valid C1/D visas that allowed them to work on their ships. None was attempting to enter the US by leaving their ships. All of the seafarers were subject to erratic accusations ranging from clicking on email links to affiliating with African child trafficking rings to possessing photos of naked children.

None of the seafarers interviewed by Rappler were ever presented with evidence to support CBP’s accusations. One seafarer, however, was shown a video he had taken of a seal swimming in the ocean as supposed “evidence” of child pornography.

Alex, a manager who has worked on cruise ships for more than 23 years, was accused of possessing child pornography, and also of terrorist activity through alleged involvement with Mexican drug cartels.
“I had no idea where this was coming from,” Alex said. “I just said no, of course I’ve never been involved in either of those things!”

Mark, a cook, said he was accused of clicking a link in a child pornography email, but when he asked to see the email, CBP never complied. CBP then pressured him to sign a form and threatened him with a US$100,000 fine.

Feeling he had no other choice, Mark signed, only to discover that the form had no mention of child pornography. All it said was he was “likely to jump ship” and that he was working illegally, even though he had a valid working visa.

Jordan, an assistant cook, was never even accused of a crime. He was just told there was a problem with his visa and then deported. He is now facing the same discrimination as the other seafarers for having a revoked US visa.

James, a motorman with more than 20 years experience working on cruise ships, believes that Filipinos are being deported using any reason that CBP can get away with, and not exactly for the sake of collective punishment.

“Filipinos are the main targets because they know that our government is weak,” said James. “The US has a quota to fill and they know the Philippine government is not going to do anything to protest.”
James was able to obtain a new contract on a Chinese ship, but only because he happened to have a contact in China. “The government didn’t help me at all,” he said.

blocks.caption: Ellene Sana, executive director of the Center for Migrant Advocacy

blocks.text: Last year, approximately 90 deported seafarers were able to avail of monetary support from a newly created government Aksyon Fund. But according to Myrla Baldonado of PWC, this fund dried up and left the majority of deported seafarers without assistance.
Reynaldo, who is now working in Europe thanks to support from his manning agency, also expressed disappointment in the Philippine government.

“The DMW’s promises never came to fruition,” he said. “They excel at making promises and putting on appearances when the harsh reality is, it felt like a complete show just to make it look like they were doing their jobs.”
Advocates from the Save Our Seafarers coalition are hoping this will change.

At the September 21st forum, representatives from the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) both pledged a renewed commitment to helping deported seafarers.

“This situation is mas maingay, mas delikado (louder, more dangerous) because of our Middle East crisis. But this forum has triggered interest to let the government hear you again,” said DMW Assistant Secretary Ogie San Diego.
“We have to dwell on your innocence. The DMW wants to add personal welfare officers in every port, but we have to be careful about encroaching on the sovereignty of the US.”

OWWA lawyer Jasmine Ann Gapatan echoed the need to respect US sovereignty, but committed to individual case management for affected seafarers. She also announced new skills training for land-based employment including virtual assistant, barista, and digital content training.

Later that same afternoon, Senator Risa Hontiveros delivered a privilege speech on deported seafarers that urged the DMW and the Department of Foreign Affairs to account for every deported seafarers’ needs.

“A person should not lose an entire career simply because an allegation followed him home,” said Hontiveros. “The fight against child sexual abuse and the protection of due process are not opposing principles. We can, and must, do both.”
Ellene of CMA praised the senator’s speech saying it was a message of “assurance that the Philippine government heard [the seafarers’] cry for justice loud and clear.”
Hontiveros also called for stronger mechanisms for consular intervention, and pressing for compliance with mandatory consular notification.

This is a practice that could have helped James. At the time of his removal, CBP was also removing a Norwegian worker from the ship. But an HR representative from Viking Ocean Cruises called the Norwegian embassy, and as a result the Norwegian worker was allowed to stay. James did not receive the same treatment.

But James is one of the lucky ones who was able to find new work. A few others were helped by E-GMP International and North Seas, rare manning agencies who have actually stood up for their kababayan (compatriot). But the majority of deported seafarers are still searching for new contracts and facing discrimination along the way.

Carl and his wife Mica, who met while working in cruise ship casinos, have been unable to secure new contracts since April 2025. Carl was deported due to false accusations, and Mica was later forced to resign.
“The ordeal we went through was full of torment and terror,” said Carl. “More than a year has passed and it’s still a struggle. All we ask is for the chance to rebuild what was taken from us.”

Royal Caribbean regularly awarded Carl and Mica Employees of the Month while they worked on the ship. Given their skills and how popular they were with passengers and managers alike, Carl feels strongly that they are now being discriminated against given the false accusations of possessing child pornography. He appealed to both the government and manning agencies to do more for all deported seafarers.
“You call us OFWs the modern day heroes, but even heroes need help,” said Carl. “We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for fairness, due process, and protection.”

There is foreign precedent for the protection Filipino seafarers are demanding. In September 2025, 300 South Koreans with valid B-1 visas were swept up in an immigration raid at a US auto plant. They were similarly placed in shackles, held in detention, and forced to sign documents they didn’t understand.

The South Korean government took swift action, with the president condemning the raid and the foreign minister flying to Washington within days. This diplomatic action led to a reversal from Trump, changes to the US visa system, and an offer to return to work for all Koreans affected by the raid.

Will the Philippine government follow South Korea’s example and step up its defense of Filipino seafarers? Or will more Filipino heroes have to suffer the consequences of what lawyer Ian Seruelo calls US immigration enforcement’s “groundless assaults on people’s rights”?
According to US Customs and Border Patrol, there is no deadline for Operation Tidal Wave, and it may even be extended to other ships, including cargo ships, in the future. – Rappler.com
Seafarers’ names have been changed to protect their privacy and prevent potential discrimination by government or manning agencies.

articles.title: Velasco camp rejects ex-aide’s P2-billion cash delivery claims involving Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The camp of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco has rejected claims by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered billions of pesos in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and…

blocks.text: September 27, 2026 | 1:48pm

In this photo uploaded on Facebook on July 30, 2025 shows Vice President Sara Duterte and former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco visiting the Talawan and Argao Elementary Schools in Marinduque as part of the PanSarap Project and PagbaBAGo Campaign.
Lord Allan Velasco via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The camp of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco on Saturday, September 26, has rejected claims by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered billions of pesos in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and members of her family on Velasco’s instructions.

Lawyer Rowell Ilagan, Velasco’s spokesperson, described Gracioso’s account as “designed and fabricated,” saying it does not match verifiable events, including the COVID-19 pandemic and Velasco’s period as House speaker.

According to GMA News, Gracioso claimed he served as Velasco’s head of security from 2018 until 2022 and delivered cash-filled suitcases to Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte and Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte.
He estimated that he delivered more than P2 billion to the vice president in more than 20 separate deliveries.
Gracioso’s sworn affidavit detailed alleged cash deliveries ranging from P20 million to P50 million to various locations in Metro Manila, Davao and other areas.
The National Bureau of Investigation is looking into the allegations.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said the agency subjected Gracioso to a polygraph test and was able to validate some of his statements through other means.
VP Sara denies receiving money
Duterte denied knowing Gracioso and receiving money from him.
“I do not know Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., nor have I ever received any money from him,” Duterte said in a statement on Saturday.
She said her lawyers were waiting for an official copy of Gracioso’s affidavit from the NBI before preparing cases against him.
“Once we are done dismantling the lies contained in his testimony, it will end up in the trash bin—just like the one from Ramil Madriaga,” she said.
Madriaga had previously been identified by Gracioso as Duterte’s alleged bagman and aide. Duterte has also denied knowing him.
The vice president described Gracioso’s allegations as “another media stunt” aimed at reviving what she called a “faltering impeachment case.”
Duterte also accused the Marcos administration of trying to remove her from office, pursue Charter Change, prevent the 2028 elections and stay in power.
Velasco camp hits back
Ilagan said Velasco’s government record was “untainted with corruption” and rejected the allegations against the former speaker and his wife.

“The ‘one-size-fits-all’ narrative by this individual seems to be designed and fabricated to attack as many targets as it can while being inconsistent with verifiable events, that is, the Covid-19 pandemic, Atty. Velasco’s period of service as speaker, other details, and even basic common sense,” Ilagan said.

Ilagan also questioned Gracioso’s personal and professional record, citing what he described as misconduct and disciplinary sanctions, including his recent dismissal from the Philippine National Police over criminal acts.
He urged the public to be “more circumspect” in assessing the report as Velasco’s camp considers possible legal action against Gracioso and the publisher.
The House prosecution panel, meanwhile, said Gracioso’s claims should be taken seriously, saying they could be relevant to allegations of unexplained wealth raised in Duterte’s impeachment case.

articles.summary: Stephen Curry reportedly takes a deal $20 million below the max to give the Warriors more salary-cap flexibility next offseason

blocks.text: SHOOTING GREAT. Stephen Curry in action for the Golden State Warriors.
NBA History X page
Stephen Curry reportedly takes a deal $20 million below the max to give the Warriors more salary-cap flexibility next offseason
The Golden State Warriors and Stephen Curry agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension, ESPN reported.
The deal, according to the report, includes a player option for the 2028-29 season.

ESPN also reported that Curry will receive $20 million less than what he could have maxed out at to give the Warriors more salary-cap space for next offseason. According to the report, Curry and the team had been working on several contract ideas once he became eligible for a two-year, $136.7 million max deal in August.
If Curry plays through the 2028-29 campaign, it would be his 20th season, all with the Warriors.

The 38-year-old was limited to 43 games last season, with much of the time missed because of a lingering knee injury. Nonetheless, Curry averaged 26.6 points, 4.4 made three-pointers, and 11.3 attempted 3-pointers per game — all above his career averages.

A 12-time All-Star drafted seventh overall out of Davidson in 2009, Curry has two scoring titles, two MVP awards, and a Finals MVP award to go with four NBA championships. However, the Warriors are coming off a 37-45 season, their worst in a non-shortened season since going 36-46 in 2010-11.
Earlier this week, Curry said he wanted “no drama” with the contract talks, particularly with camp opening on Tuesday, September 29.

“The idea of getting back to work is exciting,” Curry said Wednesday, September 23. “I feel like I’ve taken advantage of the offseason. I feel like there’s no hesitation about where I’m at physically going in. … But I’m excited about getting back to work.”
Curry has career averages of 24.8 points, 4.0 made three-pointers, and 9.4 attempted per game. The latter two marks are NBA records, as is his career .912 free throw percentage.
He also holds the NBA career marks for three-pointers made (4,248) and attempted (10,073). – Rappler.com

articles.title: Undercover police officer lied to spycops inquiry about sexual relationship
articles.summary:
Officer forced to admit relationship with woman lasting at least six months while working under fake name Dave Evans

An undercover police officer who infiltrated leftwing and animal rights…

blocks.text: An undercover police officer who infiltrated leftwing and animal rights campaign groups appears to have lied to the spycops inquiry when he claimed he did not have a sexual relationship as part of his deployment.
The officer who used the fake name Dave Evans had originally testified that he did not have any relationships while using his fake identity.

But this week, he was forced to admit to the inquiry that he did have a relationship with a woman that lasted at least six months. Under questioning, he said it was “possible” that it could have continued for two years, but could not recall how long.
Evans made the admission after campaigners drew evidence of the relationship to the attention of the spycops inquiry.

A central issue of the inquiry is how the undercover officers frequently had sexual relations with women, but did not disclose to them their true identities. Four of the spies fathered, or are alleged to have fathered, children with women they met while working undercover.

Evans was one of about 139 undercover officers who were sent by their police superiors to spy on tens of thousands of mainly leftwing activists over more than four decades. He infiltrated the Socialist Workers party and animal rights groups including London Animal Action between 1998 and 2005.
In his first statement to the inquiry signed four years ago, he wrote: “I did not engage in any sexual activity whilst in my undercover identity.”
But in a second statement that he signed this year, he admitted that “with the benefit of hindsight”, he should have disclosed that he had a relationship with a woman known as Olivia.

He made the admission after the inquiry had been told about his relationship with Olivia by campaigners. This evidence was mainly supplied by Helen Steel, a social justice campaigner who was a defendant in the celebrated McLibel case.

Steel was herself deceived into a two-year relationship by another undercover officer, John Dines. She spent 18 years searching for Dines; at one point senior police officers spent £2.5m of public funds to relocate him to ensure that she did not find him.
Evans was asked by Don Ramble, a barrister at the inquiry, if he had lied in his first statement. He replied:”I accept that it was not completely truthful with hindsight.”
He said he had not originally disclosed the relationship to the inquiry “because she was not an activist nor part of any target group, I did not feel this was relevant”.
after newsletter promotion

During his covert deployment, Evans pretended to be a landscape gardener as part of his false persona. He met Olivia in 1998 when he attended a college course in his fake identity. At no point did he reveal to her that he was actually a police officer.
The inquiry heard evidence that Evans and Olivia together attended social events with animal rights campaigners and at least one demonstration. Olivia is not giving evidence to the inquiry.

The spycops inquiry has been scrutinising wide-ranging wrongdoing committed by undercover officers. The government is considering whether the remaining stages of the inquiry, which has been running for more than a decade, should continue in a different format.
Victims of the surveillance however say that any move to cut short the inquiry would result in a cover-up.

articles.title: ‘I turbocharged my career then pressed eject’: why couples are getting divorced later
articles.summary:
Financial pressures, legal changes and shifting attitudes may help explain why couples are staying married for longer

“We don’t know anyone whose marriage hit the skids after just a few…

blocks.text: “We don’t know anyone whose marriage hit the skids after just a few years,” Celia said, reflecting on her divorce. “Everyone seemed to cling on to their relationships for as long as they possibly could.”

It took Celia two years to initiate divorce after realising her 12-year marriage wasn’t going anywhere – and the latest figures show this experience is increasingly common, with marriages that end in divorce now lasting longer than at any point since records began.

“I approached it very methodically,” the AI analyst said. “I knew that women almost always end up financially worse off after divorce, especially where there are children concerned, so I took the time I needed to turbocharge my career before pressing ‘eject’.”
It helped, Celia said, that she and Martyn, her former husband, had been in their 40s when they got married.

“Because we were older and wiser, we took the time to try to mend our relationship instead of rushing off to start a new life,” she said. “When that didn’t work, Martyn was mature enough to know it was best for the children, me and us that he subtly left me alone to get to where I needed to be before we formally called time on the relationship.”

According to figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released this week, the median length of a marriage before it ends in divorce reached 13 years in England and Wales in 2025. The figure for opposite-sex marriages has risen from 12.7 years in 2023 and a low of 8.9 years in 1985.

At the same time, the proportion of couples divorcing during their first decade of marriage has fallen sharply. Among couples who married in 2015, an estimated 16.3% had divorced by their 10th anniversary, compared with 24.7% of those who married in 1995.

The ONS research does not give any answers as to why marriages are ending later. But it does suggest several hypotheses, including that couples may delay the legal end of their relationships until they can afford what comes next.

Prof Emma Hitchings, the deputy head of the University of Bristol law school, who led the Fair Shares project, a nationally representative study in England and Wales examining how divorcing couples divide their money and property, said: “Divorce may have become legally easier, with the advent of no-fault divorces, but separating one household into two has not.”
She said that the longer a couple stayed together, the more tightly entwined – and harder to untangle – their finances became.

“Every financial aspect of divorce is harder,” she said. “From higher tax and mortgage rates, childcare and school fees – as well as the general cost of living. Then throw in the cuts to legal aid for almost all private family law proceedings in England and Wales, and you can see why couples need to spend more time trying to calculate how they can feasibly afford to separate – which may well account for why marriages are lasting longer before divorce.”

Celia said she and Martyn had a number of friends who also broke up after marriages of similar lengths. “It was the oddest thing. But we have three groups of friends, across Europe and in the US, who went through divorces after marriages of a decade or more.”
The research bears out Celia’s experience. In the US, the Pew Research Center found that the median length of marriages ending in divorce rose from 10 years in 2008 to 12 years in 2023.

Germany’s federal statistics office put the average length of marriages ending in divorce at 14.6 years in 2025. In the Netherlands, the figure was 14.7 years. Belgium’s statistics office recorded a median of 12.03 years in 2024.

The figures are not directly comparable as countries collect and present divorce statistics differently. But the broad pattern of marriages lasting longer before divorce is not solely a British phenomenon.

Anne Barlow, professor emeritus of family law and policy at the University of Exeter, said there was a curious feature of the British figures. “No-fault divorce, introduced in 2022, made the legal route out of marriage more straightforward – but there has been no corresponding rush into divorce,” she said.

One possibility was that knowing you could leave made it easier to wait, said Dr Alexander Maine, a senior lecturer at the City law school who leads a research project called: “Queer families and the law after ‘I do’.”

“Another is that no-fault divorce could allow couples to work through a separation without the acrimony that previously accompanied assigning blame,” he said. “If there is no need to prove fault, there may be less pressure to bring the marriage to an immediate legal end.”

Greg Ceely, the ONS’s head of population life events, emphasised that until more research was done, these all remained hypotheses. “The change can’t definitively be attributed to any one thing – or any number of things – because there are so many social and economic factors that could also affect the trend,” he said.

Certainly, experts find no problem in pointing to other possible reasons for marriages lasting longer before divorce, from disruption to the family courts affecting the timing of divorces in the years around Covid, as well as influencing the duration figures, to the 2022 changes introducing a minimum 20-week period between the start of proceedings and application for a final order.

Julia Carter, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of the West of England, Bristol, who is researching couples living together after divorce or separation, said wider global and environmental uncertainty was also having an impact.

“I hear people saying that even if their marriage isn’t great, they don’t want to introduce uncertainty into their homes as well, especially if there are children in the relationship who are having to negotiate this unstable world outside their family homes,” she said.

Carter pointed to the fact that women remain overwhelmingly the main instigators of divorce. “So if we’re saying that people are waiting later to get divorce, we’re actually saying that women are waiting longer in order to get divorced. So you’ve got to look at what’s changed for women,” she said.

In the 1990s and 2000s, she said, “society was all about female empowerment, girl power, Sex and the City, and ‘let’s go out and grab our opportunities’. But there’s been a rolling back from that kind of positioning, especially for women, because we’ve been through so many crises since then: economic, environmental, political, jobs.

“I think we can see the impact of that in intimate family lives where there’s an embedding of marriage as a kind of refuge, a place of long-term stability and security for couples – and especially for women,” she said. “That has reignited a reluctance to go through divorce.”

The ONS’s same-sex figures give a different set of questions. The median duration of same-sex marriages ending in divorce was 7.5 years for male couples and 6.6 years for female couples in 2025. The figures need to be treated cautiously because same-sex marriage was introduced in England and Wales only in 2014, meaning the pool of marriages that could have reached divorce is still relatively young.
But the ONS says the 6.6-year figure for female couples is nevertheless the highest recorded since the first same-sex divorces in 2015.

Maine suggested that same-sex couples might have particular reasons for taking marriage seriously. “Marriage equality was something many gay people spent so many years campaigning for very hard,” he said. “Because of that, divorce in the LGBT community sometimes carries an additional sense of having failed not just the relationship but the whole community.”

Brienna Perelli-Harris, a professor of demography at the University of Southampton and director of the UK Generations and Gender Survey, suggested a more fundamental change that might underpin the change: the rise of cohabitation.

More than 90% of people in Britain cohabited before marrying, said Perelli-Harris, whose research across 10 European countries found that an increasing proportion of first partnerships were ending before marriage.

“Marriage may therefore be becoming a more selective institution,” she said. “Couples who move in together and discover that the relationship does not work can separate without ever marrying. Those who stay together and eventually marry are, my research shows, the couples who are happiest.”

articles.title: When the lepa lights up, Tawi-Tawi tells its story
articles.summary: At the Philippines’ southern edge, a festival of boats, dance, music, and light offers a glimpse of a maritime culture deeply rooted in community

items: Tawi-Tawi, Philippines, is characterized by its untouched beauty and strong maritime culture, with communities closely tied to the sea.
The Lepa Festival, part of the province's founding anniversary, showcases vibrant boats and traditional dances, emphasizing the cultural heritage of the Sama communities.
The event highlights the importance of the lepa as a symbol of maritime heritage, with performances and decorations reflecting a living culture rather than a mere spectacle.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
BONGAO, Philippines — From the plane, Tawi-Tawi first appears in blue.

As the aircraft descends toward Sanga-Sanga Airport, the Sulu Sea fills the window, broken by islands, reefs, and strips of green. For someone coming from the mountains of Northern Luzon, the landscape feels almost like another country.
But what strikes you first is not distance. It is how much of Tawi-Tawi still feels untouched by the kind of tourism that can reshape a place before visitors have learned to understand it.
The sea is everywhere. Boats are everywhere. Communities remain closely tied to the water. You see the beauty, and you hope it stays that way.
On my first evening in the province, I was told there was an event at the port. I went. The masts were the first things I saw.
They rose above the crowd in the fading light, ornate wooden forms visible from a distance before the boats themselves came into view. Up close, the waterfront was a burst of color.

Red, yellow, green, pink, blue, and gold streamed from the boats. Cloth stretched from tall masts toward the bows. Flags fluttered above carved hulls. Decorative panels, umbrellas, lights, and patterns made each vessel distinct.
This was the Lepa Festival, part of the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi, the province’s founding anniversary celebration. Then the music started.

blocks.caption: LEPA ON DISPLAY. A brightly decorated lepa joins the Lepa Festival in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi, on September 24, 2026, as part of the 53rd Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Almost every boat seemed to have its own sound system. Songs overlapped across the water as dancers moved on narrow decks, surrounded by musicians, children, and performers waiting their turn.
The noise was immense. So was the energy. Amid it all, the dancers held your attention.

Their movements were controlled and fluid, especially in the hands and wrists. Some of the women wore long silver fingernail extensions that gave every gesture more shape and drama. Men and children danced alongside them.
The performances drew from igal, a traditional dance associated with Sama communities, known for expressive movements of the hands, arms, and body.
Even in the din, the dancers moved with remarkable composure. The boats themselves carried another story.

blocks.caption: IGAL. Dancers perform igal during the Lepa Festival in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi.

blocks.text: The lepa is more than a festival vessel. Traditionally, it served as home, transport, and livelihood for Sama Dilaut communities whose lives were closely connected to the sea.
Many families later moved into stilt houses along the coast, but the lepa remains one of the strongest symbols of that maritime heritage.
Beneath the lights and decorations were carved hulls, elaborate wooden forms, long sweeps of cloth, and craftsmanship passed down over generations.
There were LED lights and generators, too. This was not an attempt to freeze culture in the past. It was culture being carried into the present.
Nothing about the festival felt like heritage placed neatly on display for outsiders.

People were dancing on the boats. Children were performing. Musicians were playing. Crews checked ropes and lights. Families watched from the shore. Spectators took photos and videos, but the boats still felt like community spaces rather than props.
The pride was unmistakable.

blocks.caption: HERITAGE UNDER THE MOON. An ornate masthead rises above a lepa during the 53rd Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebration in Bongao, with the evening moon visible in the background.

blocks.text: Entries came from different municipalities across Tawi-Tawi, with some supported by local officials.
As darkness settled over Bongao, the crowd thickened along the waterfront, and the tall masts formed a colorful skyline over the port.
Then came the countdown. Generators were switched on. One by one, the lepa lit up!
Green, purple, blue, red, and white lights traced the hulls, masts, carvings, and cloth. Their reflections shimmered across the dark water.
Phones went up. Children pressed closer to the front. The dancers kept moving. For a few minutes, the entire waterfront seemed to glow.

Governor Yshmael “Mang” Sali and Vice Governor Al-Syed Sali were among the provincial officials present, along with mayors, members of the Bangsamoro Parliament, and other local leaders who also served as judges.
But the officials were not the center of the night. The boats were. More importantly, the people who built, decorated, sailed, danced on, and gathered around them were.
Hja. Elmasia Madjilon, Tawi-Tawi commissioner of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, described the lighting of the lepa as something larger than spectacle.
“We are not just simply lighting a traditional vessel,” she told the crowd. “We are bringing life to a story that has traveled across generations.”
She spoke of the lepa as a vessel carrying knowledge of boatmaking, navigation, art, and a way of life shaped by the waters surrounding the islands.
“Every form, every design, and every meter carries the memory and wisdom of our ancestors,” she said.

blocks.caption: YOUNG DANCERS. Children perform traditional dance movements aboard and beside decorated lepa during the festival in Bongao, showing how cultural traditions continue to be passed on to younger generations.

blocks.text: Standing beside the boats, that was easy to understand. Heritage here was not confined to a museum. It was in the carved wood, the dancers’ hands, the children learning the movements, and the people who still knew how to build, decorate, and explain the vessels.
Festivals can sometimes reduce culture to spectacle.
There was certainly spectacle in Bongao that night: bright lights, competing sound systems, prizes, judges, and hundreds of phones pointed toward the water. But the celebration never felt hollow.
It felt communal, joyful, and rooted in place. Coming from the Cordillera, I found something familiar in that.
The landscapes could not be more different, but communities in the North also carry traditions while negotiating a rapidly changing world.
In the mountains, identity is often tied to land, ritual, weaving, memory, and place.
In Tawi-Tawi, much of that story is carried by the sea.
And on my first night in the Philippines’ southernmost province, those stories glowed on the water, one lepa after another. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Two Pronged] Our undergraduate interns are a nightmare
articles.summary: 'This year, I decided to expand our internship program to include AB (undergraduate) seniors in our internship. It is a nightmare and we will never do it again.'

blocks.text: Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.
Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.
Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

I am the head of an HR dept in a mid size hospital in Metro Manila. As part of my position and for the past 15 years, I have been in charge of internship programs for graduate students enrolled in the allied medical fields (OT, MT, etc).
This year, I decided to expand our internship program to include AB (undergraduate) seniors in our internship.

It is a nightmare and we will never do it again. At first the undergrad interns showed such promise: not as scared as the older graduates to speak up their minds. But then they started expecting their opinions to be “respected” which really means to be accepted as truth, even if they have no research or past clinical experience to back these up.
Worse, they do not have the amor propio (self respect) to apologize or even be embarrassed when they are caught inventing their test results.
They even complain that they are “triggered” when our staff scold them for things that graduate students accept, apologize for, and try to do better.

We want to stop this internship program for undergraduates but the owner of the hospital does not. The kudos he receives for this is so much that I think that (and not the program) is what he resists losing.
Please help.– Aimee
Dear Aimee,

You are clearly unhappy with the quality of the current batch of undergraduate interns that your company has hired. However, if it is in fact the case that the owner of the company is determined to maintain the program, then there is presumably little or nothing that you can do to cancel future intakes.

That said, there are other avenues you can explore. I imagine there is a selection process which you can use to weed out those applicants who demonstrate the qualities above that you find unacceptable, always supposing that the interns are unwilling to change their ways.
In addition, when individual interns reach the end of their internships, the company can simply decide not to employ them further.

A problem may develop if the company owner relies on some of these interns becoming full time employees. The fact that none successfully graduates will give you the opportunity to discuss the unsuitability of the present intake and the sustainability of an AB senior intern program, at least as it is structured now, and support your view that AB seniors do not align with your corporate requirements.
An additional argument in your favor must be that no company should be keen to employ people who are willing to invent test results and not take responsibility when caught out.

At the end of the day, your owner may come round to the view that an internship program that ultimately does not benefit his company is a luxury he can ill afford, whatever the supposed kudos involved.
Best wishes,– JAF Baer
Thank you very much for your letter. Thank you too, Mr Baer, for adding the perspective needed about how companies really work for those of us who have never worked in one.

When I first read your letter, I thought it might mean simply underscoring the differences between Gen Z and Gen Y (millennials). These would include what research backs up as “typically gen Z” and “typically Gen Y.”
Usually, a Gen Z person is anyone born between 2012 and 1996 (ages 14 to 29 in 2026).

This would then include most of both the BA and MA graduates; most MA students are usually Gen Z-ers themselves. So any differences between your MA graduates (older Gen Z-er’s) and your BA graduates may just be differences between the oldest among the Gen Z-ers and the not-so-old.

An alternative explanation is that your perception of the differences may also be a function of your expectations. This anticipation of expanding your program to include undergraduate seniors in your internship must have garnered some attention at least among other hospitals. Hence, the kudos given the owner of yours. Kudos he may be reluctant to lose — especially after so short a time.
It is tempting to “demonize” a group because their characteristics are so different from previous interns and much more difficult to adjust to.
Perhaps, the excitement of the new expansion encouraged you to focus solely on the good that could come from it, and minimize the possible problems.

It would be understandable to assure oneself that: “Nothing major could possibly go wrong! These (already) senior undergrads are just a year younger than most of the interns we already have in our program.”
But I think problems arose, thus things did go wrong and having such high expectations made them seem worse than they really were.

It is easy to look for a scapegoat when plans go awry and much easier when problems that arise are so closely connected (at least in time) to the new group that just came in. But it could only mean that new procedures are always difficult to adjust to. It could even be that this particular group of AB seniors have quirks much more difficult to take.

Mr Baer’s suggestion to improve your selection process might be most important. It might not necessarily mean the next bunch of interns you decide to bring in will be perfect, but I think they will be far better than those you already have.
At the risk of sounding naïve, I doubt your ending this expansion immediately will be well received either by your boss, but also by your cohorts.
Another way of dealing with this problem is to concentrate on yourself.
The most important is to try and shift your nervous system from one that is, at present, on high alert and thus reactive, and take slow, deep breaths that will calm you.

Another calming possibility is acknowledging your feelings: Is it frustration? Shock? Extreme disappointment? Or merely confusion? If you can do this without judging or berating yourself, (after all, we cannot be responsible for our feelings, just for what we do with them) you will be in a better state to decide what the best next step might be.
Finally, avoid immediate assumptions: Remind yourself that an unexpected difference is not automatically a catastrophe or a personal threat.

These three suggestions will not solve all your problems, but I hope will ease some of the worry that block us from choosing the most rational decision. It takes a lot of courage to try and improve a system that was already running smoothly. It takes even more courage to recognize and admit that, in the beginning at least, it seemed not the best decision to make.
And yet, you did both of that! Kudos to you!
With every best wish!– MG Holmes
Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.
