articles.title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
articles.summary: China's economy and tech have developed at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".
Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.
And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.
China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.

"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.
"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."

She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".

Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.

blocks.caption: Image caption, About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently

blocks.text: About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently

In Sinapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging.
It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.

These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times".
"Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore.
"But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it."
He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.

Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.
China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says

blocks.text: Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says
Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air.

"The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.
This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers.

One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."
Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."

Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures

blocks.text: Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures

Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.

Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."

And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.
Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.

They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.

Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects

blocks.text: Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects

Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.

Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.
The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home.
"When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."
About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".
Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.
But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity.
"If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

articles.title: Australian backlash to datacentres is faux import from US, officials say: ‘We are not the United States’
articles.summary: Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US Australian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s…

blocks.text: Australian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s growing resentment of AI datacentres is an inauthentic import from the United States.

Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. They say the burgeoning negative reaction is being tainted and inflamed by a heated US debate that has arrived down under via social media feeds.

When the backlash began in earnest in the United States last year, it echoed slowly in Australia. In 2026, though, it has exploded into national conversation across the country, leading to calls for a national moratorium, community protests, three government inquiries, state frameworks being developed and the Australian government moving to set the rules for how the datacentres can be built, and how they consume energy and water.

Australian state governments, desperate for economic growth, have been broadly welcoming of the investment for the new centres, in some cases overriding local council approval processes, given the size of the projects being developed.

In July, Victoria’s then-minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, boasted that his state was second only to New South Wales in terms of datacentres, and was outstripping Australia’s most populous state in growth for new centres. He expressed concern that the growing resentment toward new developments was a result of US social media influence.

blocks.caption: Protest signs as Donald Trump speaks at the General Motors proving ground testing facility in Milford, Michigan, on 27 July. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We’re seeing some US states move to ban new large datacentres. And those campaigns and mega-developments in the US shape public opinion in Australia,” he said. “Because when it’s on your phone, you think it’s right here, or you think it might just come here.”
The minister declared: “We are not the United States. Our planning, energy and water systems are much more carefully monitored, managed and regulated.”
Leaders in the datacentre sector have also complained about the backlash, calling it misleading and disingenuous.
“Australia’s datacentre debate is being fought on America’s facts,” Belinda Dennett, the head of the peak lobby group for the sector, Data Centres Australia, declared in a speech in March.
Dennett said reactions to datacentres from everyday people range from curiosity to confusion and fear, and the news around the sector was “alarming”.

“The industry is depicted as energy vampires, water hogs and job killers,” she said. “The problem is that most of those headlines originate in the United States, where the industry is operating at a completely different scale, under completely different market rules. They are being transplanted wholesale into Australian debates as though the contexts were interchangeable.”
Dennett said the US has 5,400 datacentres, with 53.7 gigawatts of total capacity, compared with 252 in Australia with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. Measurements of the number of US datacentres vary.

“When people read about datacentres straining the grid, driving up bills and consuming vast amounts of water, they are reading about America’s challenges, applied uncritically to an Australian market that bears almost no resemblance to it,” she said.
What Dennett omitted was that Australia, with a population of 28 million, has just under one datacentre per 100,000 people, compared with 1.5 per 100,000 people in the US, population 342.7 million.

blocks.caption: Protesters outside the Senate inquiry into datacentre regulatory frameworks in Melbourne, Australia, on 23 September. Photograph: James Ross/AAP

blocks.text: The pace of datacentre construction is increasing rapidly in Australia, with several large datacentres with 1 gigawatts or more capacity in the planning.

Trending videos on TikTok and Instagram highlight major local community concerns including a 2.4 gigawatt centre planned for outer Melbourne, and a 2 gigawatt gas-powered centre in the Northern Territory.
after newsletter promotion

That is the equivalent of 2m households’ annual electricity consumption, said Rob Nicholls, professor and senior research associate in digital policy at the University of Sydney. The NT’s population is just over 265,000.

The Australian government – seeing the US gas boom fueled by datacentres’ demand for power – has planned to override states and ban gas being used to power centres. New rules would require datacentres’ operators to bring as much new renewable energy into the system as the centre would otherwise take.
Some experts find the backlash justified in following the US example.

“The social media input from the US is very vocal and rationally based: ‘It’s going to increase the cost of electricity and it’s going to increase the cost of water and I don’t get a benefit from it.’ And that’s a rational position,” said Nicholls.
Nicholls said the hurdle facing the Australian government is explaining to its constituents how the issues faced in the United States differ from local ones.

Legislation for the framework is unlikely to arrive until next year, and has led to calls for Australia to follow the lead of New York and implement a moratorium on new development until proper rules are in place.
Until then, there are now two state inquiries and one federal inquiry into the sector, along with the steady stream of new development applications leading to pushback from locals.

Many of Australia’s datacentres are US-owned. The federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, said that Australians may be cynical about datacentres in their communities because many of the companies that operate the facilities are not Australian. Microsoft and Amazon operate several, and OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing their own developments.

“Simply building datacentres in Australia does not necessarily mean that Australia captures the economics of AI,” he said in a speech this week. “We can supply the land, we can supply the electricity, we can host the machines, and still find that much of the value – and many of the economic rents – flow offshore.”

Charlton called for datacentre providers who want to build in Australia to enable access to compute for Australian start-ups, researchers and not-for-profits, on favourable terms, and flagged that Australia could build its own local AI capability based on open-weight models.
“We risk becoming dependent on imported intelligence itself,” Charlton said.

articles.title: Are claims of a white genocide in South Africa real?
articles.summary: Thousands of white crosses have been displayed in Washington by an Afrikaner lobby group But South Africa's new ambassador Roelf Meyer says there is not a genocide.

blocks.text: An Afrikaner lobby group has displayed thousands of white crosses on the National Mall in Washington DC, saying they represent the victims of a genocide of white people in South Africa.
But South Africa's new ambassador to the US, Roelf Meyer, says that the notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
The BBC's North America correspondent Ione Wells explains what role the US has played in the claim of a genocide.

articles.title: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.summary: Christy Spivey tells the BBC she only has more questions now police think Tasia Fortune's body was put in the tree after her death.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details

The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.
"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.

The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.
Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.
"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.
"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"
Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion.

Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.
"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."
When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".
Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.
Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction.
"Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said.
"If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does."
She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes.
Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

articles.title: Helicopter crashes outside Montreal killing all four occupants
articles.summary: Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville on Saturday afternoon.

image.caption: The helicopter was on fire when first responders arrived at the scene, police said. (Emily Blais/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville on Saturday afternoon.
Major crimes unit investigating crash
Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais off Highway 10 in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville on Saturday afternoon.
Sûreté du Québec spokesperson Brigitte Dorsainville said it happened at around 2:30 p.m. ET and the helicopter was on fire when first responders arrived.
Dorsainville said all four occupants on board were declared dead at the scene.
Police, however, were unable to provide details on the ownership of the helicopter, where it took off or the identities of the victims, citing early stages of the investigation.
The fire has since been brought under control and the SQ's major crimes unit has taken over the file.
The Transportation Safety Board of Canada is also sending a team of investigators to the site, police said.
Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville is located roughly 55 kilometres southeast of Montreal.

articles.title: Major storm in US north-east knocks out power for 100,000 and floods roads
articles.summary: Residents across New Jersey, Massachusetts, Delaware and New York without electricity as storm hits A slow-moving, powerful storm known as a nor’easter crept along the coast of the US north-east on…

blocks.text: A slow-moving, powerful storm known as a nor’easter crept along the coast of the US north-east on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to thousands of people while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.

Tens of millions of people were in the path of the storm, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. About 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.

The forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There would potentially be “a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain … over the next few days for the northeastern US”, said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service (NWS) in College Park, Maryland.
On Long Island, New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets.

In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, Kenny Formica sat at his home watching surveillance cameras showing water rising inside the marina he owns. Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4m in damage to his business.

Before the storm, Formica said, workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm’s way and parked the marina’s trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.
Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. One customer sent him a video at about 4am of his 25ft (7.6-meter) boat after it had blown off its lift.
“This is like an 8,000lb boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat – just gone,” Formica said.
In Ocean City, Maryland, heavy surf caused beach erosion, washed out fencing by the dunes and was leading to flooding.
“In all the canals, the water is up really high and coming into people’s backyards,” Jay Boyd said by telephone.

Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some east coast flights through the weekend.

Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community of Sea Bright, said the borough was bracing for winds up to 50mph (80km/h) and flooding that could reach up to 6ft (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start on Saturday and worsen by midday.

“It’s going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the north-east. “I hope I’m wrong, but that’s my gut feeling.”
Kelly added that he hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.

Peak wind gusts were expected to approach 60-65mph (97-105km/h) on Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, and about 50-55mph (80-89km/h) around Boston and 35-40mph (56-64km/h) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with the NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.
“It’s definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see,” Belk said.

Belk said nor’easters were not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season was that leaves still remain on trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn could cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.

Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60mph (96.6km/h), according to NWS. In south-eastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could be almost as powerful, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.
More than 200 flights to and from airports in Boston, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard and New York had been canceled on Friday, and more cancellations were already in place for Saturday.

Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday-afternoon game to Friday to create a split double-header. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.

articles.title: China, U.S. agree to AI dialogue, tariff cuts on $30 billion in goods during Xi visit
articles.summary: The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on $30 billion US of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping shake hands after visiting the National Archives Museum in Washington on Friday. The two countries agreed to hold a dialogue on AI benefits and risks in November. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on $30 billion US of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.
3-day summit ends with personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs

The tariff reductions would apply to U.S. exports such as agricultural goods, wood and cosmetics, as well as U.S. imports including small appliances, toys and decorations, a White House statement said on Friday.
"The two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.

The three-day summit between Xi and President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.

items: Trump cozying up to Xi Jinping could spell trouble for Canada, says Michael Kovrig

blocks.text: The two sides also agreed to set up a trade council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.

The agreement follows a move by the world's two largest economies to extend by two months a trade truce that had been due to expire on Nov. 10, allowing more time to work on ‌a potentially bigger trade deal, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday.

"This historic visit enriched the constructive and stable China-U.S. relationship, upheld the overall stability of bilateral ties, opened a new chapter in China-U.S. relations, and will have a far-reaching impact on world peace and development," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in a statement.
Dialogue on AI

On artificial intelligence, the two sides agreed to hold a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, and to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.
The White House said that the leaders had agreed to use the term "super intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence."
Trump, Xi appear chummy as White House keeps media on tight leash
In a separate statement, the Chinese ministry said that Beijing valued Washington's use of the new term.
As AI technology continues to advance, the two sides should step up exchanges and work toward consensus in line with new developments, it said.

items: Fanfare surrounds Trump-Xi summit at White House, but no breakthroughs expected

blocks.text: The two sides also agreed to support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting and the Group of 20 summit, with both leaders planning to attend the gatherings hosted by the other.

On foreign policy, the leaders agreed that Iran should fulfill its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on international waterways, both countries said.

articles.title: Private colleges around Australia offering last-minute discounts for diploma allegedly ‘misused by shonks’
articles.summary: Federal government to deregister graduate diploma of management in October over fears it was being used by ‘non-genuine’ students to remain in country Get our breaking news email , free app or daily…

blocks.text: Private colleges are offering discounts to rush students into a diploma the federal government is cancelling over concerns it is being “misused by shonks”.

The government announced in early September it would deregister the graduate diploma of management (learning) which it suspected was being used by “non-genuine” students to remain in Australia. The course is taught by close to 450 institutions, has over 15,000 students studying currently and more than 40,000 students registered for future enrolment following completion of a different vocational course.

Ads posted to social media and shared among agents and students in recent days encouraged students to join the course or expedite their start date before cancellation on 5 October. Any students already enrolled and studying by that date are allowed to complete it.

Some immigration education agents have offered promotions for the month of September, including in WhatsApp messages and texts, encouraging students to join the course or those who have a future enrolment to study now. Several ads promote discounted course fees or a free certificate of enrolment to join immediately.

One private college has sent immigration agents a promotion offering “attractive” commissions with same-day offer letters and confirmation of enrolment for students, with two “special intakes” on 21 September and 2 October – just three days before the course is cancelled.

Phil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), supported the decision to cancel the course and said it could put some private providers trying to loophole the system into financial trouble.
“The government for all the right reasons moved to stop non-genuine international students from using this course to stay in the country,” Honeywood said.
“High-quality providers will always have a place in the international education ecosystem … they would rather have these factory-type private providers out of the system for all the right reasons.”

Some education migration providers are encouraging the more than 40,000 international students with a future enrolment to start the course now before it is cancelled. Some of those students would need to do so, or choose a different course such as a bachelor’s or master’s with a high qualification level to maintain their visa conditions. That could mean completing two courses at the same time.
Students who have “packaged” a lower-level vocational course with the graduate diploma to be completed after, will need to enrol into a higher-level course to maintain their visa requirements.

One student who spoke to Guardian Australia on the condition of anonymity said they had initially come to Australia to study a bachelor’s degree but unenrolled after one semester on the advice of a migration agent to do a VET course in carpentry, followed by the graduate diploma in management. The graduate diploma and the VET course would fulfil the qualification level required to maintain a valid international student visa.
They said they were being told to commence the graduate diploma now.

“I talked to the agent, and they told me the new rules. They want me to study concurrently, [so] I can study both courses at the same time. I don’t know if I can take this much study load,” the international student said.
They said other friends doing the same course pathway were also given the same advice, and were also stressed by the potential workload.

A migration agent, who asked not to be named, said they had heard of other agents and institutions pushing students to expedite their enrolment, but they warned the government would view this suspiciously. They said they were concerned that this behaviour would damage the reputation and credibility of the rest of the sector.

They also said private institutions might look at setting up other courses such as the graduate diploma of strategic leadership that just over 34 colleges currently teach or the graduate diploma of portfolio management that is taught by just a few, that have the same visa requirement level.
after newsletter promotion
Julian Hill, the assistant minister responsible for cancelling the course, said the department and education regulator would be “closely watching student and provider behaviour”.

blocks.caption: Assistant minister for citizenship and  multicultural affairs, Julian Hill. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: “Students and providers are on notice that curious patterns of early commencement or new enrolments will be investigated and action taken against those doing the wrong thing,” Hill told Guardian Australia.

At the time of the announcement in September that the course would be deregistered, Hill said in a statement: “The Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks.”
Melanie McFarlane, New South Wales president of the Migration Institute of Australia, said some education agents were helping their students into master’s courses to maintain their visas.

“Those students needing to find an alternate course, they’re being placed by, I would say, reputable agents, into a master’s degree within the same institution where that graduate diploma was otherwise available,” she said.

“But then you’ve got the other side where there are migration agents who are potentially going out of business because of all the changes to the industry … and might be rushing students into that course in the time that they can.”
It is part of a wider crackdown by the government to curb visa-hopping and overstayers in Australia.

The government has now banned international students from starting one qualification and then transferring to a lower-value qualification which would allow them to remain in the country and work more hours instead of studying. This would help prevent a student enrolled in a bachelor’s degree from downgrading to a vocational course.
Hill said the government had also banned commissions for agents transferring students between courses in Australia.
“This has helped but the quantum and pattern of transfers remains concerning, so from next year international students looking to change providers will have to apply for [a] new visa.”

articles.title: Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly told to stop wearing keffiyeh at Sydney school sues for racial discrimination
articles.summary: Wasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A Palestinian careers…

blocks.text: A Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly directed to stop wearing a keffiyeh at a Sydney government school because it was a symbol that “may cause discord” has lodged a racial discrimination case in the federal court against the state of New South Wales.

Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School – an inner-city selective government school – alleges the then acting principal told him in 2024 that the keffiyeh was seen as a symbol of conflict. He alleges the state’s conduct is unlawful for breaching the Racial Discrimination Act.

El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh – a traditional scarf linked to the struggle for a Palestinian state for decades – at school in January 2024, three months after Hamas’ 7 October attacks and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza.

His statement of claim, filed in the federal court last month, alleges Geoffrey Denyer, the then acting school principal, met with him on 15 May 2024 and said words to the effect of “I have been directed to direct you to remove this item of clothing”, indicating to El-Haj’s keiffeyh.

blocks.caption: Wasim El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh to Sydney Girls High School in January 2024. Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: Denyer also said words to the effect of the direction had come “from above, possibly from the minister” and that action would be taken if El-Haj did not comply, the statement of claim alleges.
In an email sent the same day, after El-Haj requested the issue be laid out in writing, Denyer outlined the terms of the direction he had received.

“Consistent with the Department’s Controversial Issues and Code of Conduct policies, the staff member in question should be given clear advice, from you, that this item of clothing should not be worn at school, nor in the performance of any duties in connection with his employment. That advice should be complied with immediately,” the email said.
“It is understandable that, in such times as these, feelings and emotions are strong. However, our schools need to remain free of symbols which stir these emotions, and which may cause discord.”
El-Haj alleges that in a further conversation with Denyer he said words to the effect of “any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict”.

In August 2024, El-Haj met with Maria Serafim, a NSW Department of Education official, who detailed six anonymous concerns, including that he had worn a symbol of “partisan conflict” by wearing the keffiyeh, the statement of claim alleges.

An internal complaint El-Haj made about the direction did not lead to its withdrawal. The careers advisor appealed the decision about the complaint to the secretary of the NSW Department of Education, Murat Dizdar.

Responding to this, Dizdar upheld the school’s decision. In a letter to El-Haj in February 2025, he recognised the keffiyeh “is a garment of cultural significance for the Palestinian community” but said the department did not want to compromise the “safety, wellbeing and security in all our school communities”.

blocks.caption: Wasim El-Haj says he was told words to the effect of ‘any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict’. Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “Unfortunately, our schools are not immune to external events, such as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with the tragic loss of innocent lives,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

“Regrettably, within our school communities, some individuals and groups may seek to politicise global conflicts or others may form that perception, and as such we always remain politically neutral in public schools when such events can impact on operations.
“It is with this context that the senior officers and the school advised you to not wear the keffiyeh to school.”
El-Haj took leave from his employment from May 2024 until the end of the year and resigned from Sydney Girls High School in March 2025.
El-Haj alleges the state of NSW has engaged in unlawful conduct under section 9(1) of the Racial Discrimination Act.
The state of NSW is yet to file its defence in the federal court.
The matter is due to be next heard for a case management hearing on 3 November, federal court records show.
A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Education said it was “committed to maintaining neutral and apolitical school environments, in line with its policies.”
Guardian Australia understands the department is not able to make further comments while the matter is before court.

articles.title: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
articles.summary: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for match against Israel.

blocks.text: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.
Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match.
But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing.

As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia.
The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.

Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.
"One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference.
"They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict.

"There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]."
There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place.

A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed.

The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding.
About 13:00, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow.

More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game.
"This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said.

"This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive.
"There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion."
Later on Saturday, Bazunu posted on social media explaining his decision, one that he said he had "not taken lightly".
"I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel," he said.
"My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong.
"It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israel people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region.
"There are few times when you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe that this is one of them."
Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures.
The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game".
"All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed.
"The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead.
"We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage."
The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games.
Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see".
"Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added.
"There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland.
"We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win."
A spokesperson for the Irish governement insists any decision regarding the fixtures lie firmly at the door of the FAI and Uefa.
"The FAI had decided to play the fixtures against Israel in accordance with their obligations as members of Uefa. Following engagement with players today decision stands," they said.

"The FAI has strongly represented the views of its membership that Israel should be excluded from international football competitions, including bringing a motion to Uefa to this effect last year. The reality is that this motion was not passed by Uefa and that the FAI was obliged to fulfil the fixture."
Israel Football Association [IFA] head of communications Shlomi Barzel commended the Republic of Ireland team for confirming they will play, saying "football has won".

Barzel began Israel's news conference with a statement before requesting questions regarding the game-only were directed towards captain Dor Peretz and head coach Ran Ben-Shimon who remained on script.
"The separation between football and politics must be maintained, any other approach spell chaos," he said, confirming Israel players intend to shake hands before the game.
"The Irish football association [FAI] and the national team players did he right thing by recognising this, even if it took a bit longer than it should. Yet, it is better to be late than never.

"The one who certainly lost today are those who want to intimidate to separate and turn the football pitch into a political arena. Uefa, the IFA [Israel Football and the FAI stood strong together to prevent it."
Barzel also confirmed the IFA intend to appeal both yellow cards shown to Sayed Abu Farhi in Thursday's 3-1 defeat by Austria.
Abu Farhi was shown a second yellow for his goal celebration which Barzel insists was not mimicking the firing of a gun, but an "imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty."

articles.title: ‘Miracle on the Hudson’ pilot Chesly Sullenberger inducted into US Aviation Hall of Fame
articles.summary: Sullenberger landed a disabled passenger plane safely in the Hudson River in 2009 without any loss of life Capt Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger III – the pilot known for safely landing a US Airways…

blocks.text: Capt Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger III – the pilot known for safely landing a US Airways flight in New York City’s Hudson River during a 2009 emergency – has been inducted into the US’s National Aviation Hall of Fame, two months after he went public with an Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis.
Sullenberger, 75, received the honor during a ceremony held in Washington DC on Thursday, 17 years after he engineered what has become widely known as the Miracle on the Hudson.
His actions that day – which saved more than 150 lives – set the stage for him to be inducted alongside the six-member 2026 hall of fame class, including Nasa astronauts and aviation researchers.

Sullenberger participated in the ceremony remotely by video, saying: “I want to congratulate the other [inductees] on lifetimes of accomplishments. And I thank you for the honor of enshrinement in the National Aviation Hall of Fame.”

During his remarks, he recognized that the dramatic events of 2009 – which were eventually the basis of a Tom Hanks movie – played a major role in his enshrinement. But he made it a point to say: “My career was much more than one flight.
“From a very young age, I knew I wanted to fly airplanes. That was the beginning of a lifetime following that dream. I was so fortunate to spend an entire working lifetime doing something I loved.”

A former member of the US air force, Sullenberger was piloting US Airways Flight 1549 on 15 January 2009. The aircraft had departed New York City’s LaGuardia airport en route to Charlotte, North Carolina, carrying 150 passengers and five crew members.

Not long after takeoff, the aircraft struck a flock of birds, resulting in a total loss of thrust from both engines. Sullenberger ultimately realized that the plane would not be able to make it back to LaGuardia – so he instead landed the aircraft in the Hudson River.
All 155 people aboard survived.
Sullenberger in July disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, which had given him another way to think about public service.

“This new phase of my life has challenged what it means to be of service,” he said in a statement shared at the time. “And the answer is to speak up. It is my hope that by sharing this, other families living in the shadows with this disease will feel they too can step forward.”

Speaking in an interview on Wednesday with the ABC program Good Morning America, Sullenberger described his reaction to learning of the diagnosis. He said he experienced “all those emotions, the shock, the anger, why me?”
“We’re part of this community who are trying to make the best of a bad situation.”
Figures from the Alzheimer’s Association indicate that about 7.4 million people who are age 65 or older are living with clinical Alzheimer’s dementia. Roughly three out of four are 75 or older.
“This is a disease – not a character flaw,” his wife, Lorrie Sullenberger, said on Good Morning America. “I think we need to talk about it more openly, and maybe other people can do the same.”

articles.title: B.C. family still looking for answers 1 month after deadly Nepal flood
articles.summary: Over 1,400 bodies have been recovered and over 5,600 people remain missing — the Canadian Press reports — a month after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet…

image.caption: Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla (top left and right) have been missing for a month since a deadly flash flood hit the Nepal-Tibet border. (Submitted by Vikram Khosla)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Over 1,400 bodies have been recovered and over 5,600 people remain missing — the Canadian Press reports — a month after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet on Aug. 26.
29 Canadians remain missing after devastating August flood
One month after a deadly flooding event in Nepal, a B.C. family is among several Canadians still waiting for answers.
Global Affairs Canada said on Saturday that 29 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing.
Coquitlam, B.C., couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among them, according to family.
"We are still clueless," said Shubakshi’s cousin Vikram Khosla.
The couple lived with their two daughters — one a teenager and one in her early 20s, he said.
"We are helpless, we can’t do anything," said Khosla.

items: 2 trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods

blocks.text: He said the couple and their two daughters had been in India visiting family at the time, when Sumit and Shubakshi took a trip to the Himalayas for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.
The couple spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck, but nobody has heard from them since then, said Khosla.
He said the daughters are back in Canada and various family members are taking turns caring for them.
Why you can’t predict a disaster like Nepal’s flood | About That
The federal government says Canadian officials continue to work with authorities in Nepal and China to support efforts to locate the missing Canadians and provide assistance to affected families.
"Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be provided, and we cannot comment on what is being discussed with families," said the statement.
Global Affairs Canada would not specify how many of the missing Canadians are from B.C., but CBC News has spoken with the family of another missing couple from Port Moody — Dhaval and Megha Shah.
Despite no news on his cousin, Khosla says the family holds onto hope that they can be found.
"Everyone keeps praying every single day, hoping that maybe they are injured, maybe they are somewhere stuck and maybe we will get to hear something about them," he said.
Khosla described the couple as "beautiful souls." He said the couple took care of others and were part of a very happy family.
"It’s hard to believe that something like that happened to them," he said. "I don’t know why they had to be there at that time."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Michelle Gomez is a writer and reporter at CBC Vancouver. You can contact her at michelle.gomez@cbc.ca.
With files from Simon Little

articles.title: Powerful storm causes widespread flooding, outages in northeast U.S.
articles.summary: A slow-moving, powerful storm crept along the coast of the northeast U.S. on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to tens of thousands while whipping up big waves and heavy…

image.caption: People navigate a flooded street in Surf City, N.J., on Saturday. (Vincent Alban/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A slow-moving, powerful storm crept along the coast of the northeast U.S. on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to tens of thousands while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.
Around 100,000 customers without power as high winds, high tides, heavy rain batter region

Tens of millions of people were in the path of the nor'easter, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. Around 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.

The forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There will be "a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S.," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Md.
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water flooded the streets and inundated some homes.
Kenny Formica, owner of Surf City Marina on the Jersey Shore, was trying to keep busy Saturday as he sat at home watching water rise inside his marina through surveillance cameras.
Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4 million in damage to his business.

Ahead of the storm, Formica said workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm's way and parked the marina's trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.

items: Hawaii readies for arrival of Hurricane Nolo amid risks of catastrophic flooding

blocks.text: Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. He said one customer sent him a video around 4 a.m. showing his 25-foot (7.6-metre) boat after it had blown off its lift.
"This is like an 8,000-pound [3.6-tonne] boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat — just gone," Formica said.

In Edgewater, N.J., along the Hudson River, water had spilled into a large parking lot packed with cars. Video posted to social media showed one car nearly submerged, with just its sunroof poking above the water, as people moved other vehicles farther from the rising tides.
Storm upends flights, events

The storm forced a change of plans for many people. Hundreds of flights were cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at the popular Massachusetts tourist destinations of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.

The Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs — both gearing up for the playoffs during the final weekend of the regular Major League Baseball season — had to shuffle the schedule for their three-game series. They played a double-header Friday in Boston to try to avoid the storm. Then MLB rescheduled their finale on Sunday to occur in Florida, at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays.
Meanwhile, Ed Sheeran cancelled his high-profile concerts Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass.
Farther south, a highway closure on North Carolina's Hatteras Island scrambled Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's Saturday wedding plans.
The Virginia couple had made it onto the island before the storm, but most of their roughly 45 guests were stranded on the other side of the closure, the Island Free Press reported.
A local campground offered a new venue, cabins and an officiant, and a DJ volunteered to provide music. Organizers invited anyone on the island to come celebrate with the couple Saturday afternoon.
East Coast officials urge caution
Nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but this one is coming early in the season.
State officials along the East Coast urged people to use caution. Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer took to social media Saturday to implore people to keep an eye on the forecast.

items: Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo

blocks.text: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, but the storm will also bring heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as six metres.
"The rain is underway and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," the governor said early Saturday.

articles.title: Tenth woman's body found in South Africa suburb as police probe killings
articles.summary: The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country.

blocks.text: Police in South Africa say that they have found a woman's body in a Johannesburg suburb, the tenth in recent months.
The body was found on Saturday morning and identified by the friend with whom she had been at a bar the previous evening.

The local police commissioner said his force could not rule out the possibility that there was a serial killer on the loose, noting similarities across the 10 deaths in Ekurhuleni, as well as another in Soweto.
The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
The latest body was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg.
Police issued a statement a short while later saying crime scene investigators were at the scene gathering evidence. Officials have yet to publicly identify the victim.
The woman's friend told national broadcaster SABC that she recognised her friend's clothes from the previous night when shown a picture of the body.
"I don't know what I'm going to say to her children," she said while wiping away tears. "It's painful."
Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said that, at this early stage in the investigation, it was too soon to say whether the woman's death was linked to the others.

He told reporters that the other bodies shared a "similar victimology" that indicated a shared "modus operandi" of killing, which would allow police to determine whether this latest death was linked to the others.
"For now, it's not something which we can overrule to say there's a serial killer, but we cannot conclusively indicate as such," Lt Gen Mthombeni said.
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates - with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
But it is the nature of the recent killings around Johannesburg that has left many women there reeling from the growing death toll.
The 10 other bodies have been found in similar circumstances to one another since July. Most of them were found in Kempton Park, one neighbourhood over from Tembisa.
Many of the bodies were those of young women and almost all had suffered extreme violence prior to their deaths.
The deaths have placed pressure on the national government less than a year after ministers declared gender-based violence a national disaster.

While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.
Three men appeared in court earlier this week accused of being involved in one of the nine murders, with police working to track down others who may have been involved.

articles.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
articles.summary: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

image.caption: Tech giant Google has several data centers in Europe Image: Patrick Scheiber/IMAGO

blocks.text: Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.

This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.

According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.
What happens when data centers lose power?
Massive water consumption

The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.

They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.

This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

blocks.caption: Several data centers are currently under construction in EuropeImage: Maksim Zabarovskii/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas

Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.

However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.

And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.

blocks.caption: Hundreds protested against a Google data center saying that AI needed democracy Image: APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.

In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.

Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.
Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.

This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.
Data centers face backlash from US communities

Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.
For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.
Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

blocks.caption: Irish writer Sally Rooney spearheaded a successful campaign against the building of a data center in IrelandImage: Ullstein/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Carlos Yulo shows support for Alex Eala, EJ Obiena ahead of Asian Games campaigns
articles.summary: Double Olympic champion Carlos Yulo expressed confidence in fellow Filipino athletes Alex Eala and EJ Obiena as they prepare to begin their respective campaigns in the 2026 Asian Games in…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 2:05am

Double Olympic gold medalist Carlos Yulo has backed fellow Filipino athletes Alex Eala and EJ Obiena as they prepare to begin their respective campaigns at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
Yulo, who wrapped up his Asian Games campaign with two gold medals in artistic gymnastics, said he believes Eala and Obiena have what it takes to succeed in the continental competition.

“Ako, naniniwala ako na kayang-kaya nila ’to. Grabe. ’Yung mga spirit ng mga ’yun... pag pinanood mo sila talaga, doon mo malalaman ’yung puso ng Pilipino,” Yulo said in an interview with JP Soriano of GMA News.
(I believe they can definitely do this. Their spirit is incredible... when you watch them, that’s when you truly see the heart of the Filipino.)
“Ito ’yung malakas pumuso talaga ang mga atleta natin (Our Filipino athletes really have a lot of heart),” he added.
Yulo also said he has been praying for Eala and Obiena, whom he considers friends, hoping they win and remain safe throughout their competitions.
“And siyempre, mga kaibigan po natin sila. Always pinagdadasal ko sila na manalo. And siyempre, maging safe po. Alam kong nasa magandang kondisyon sila ngayon,” Yulo said.
(And of course, they are our friends. I always pray for them to win and, of course, to stay safe. I know they are in good condition right now.)
The 26-year-old gymnast became the Philippines’ first double gold medalist in the Aichi-Nagoya Games after ruling the men’s floor exercise and vault finals.

Yulo won the floor exercise gold on Sept. 24 with a score of 14.666, giving the Philippines its first gold medal of the Games. He followed it with another gold in the vault final the next day, posting an average score of 14.599.
The victories gave Yulo his first two Asian Games gold medals, adding to his two Olympic gold medals from the 2024 Paris Games.

Eala, meanwhile, is set to begin her Asian Games tennis campaign after receiving a first-round bye. The 21-year-old Filipina is the highest-ranked player in the women's singles field and will face the winner of Thailand's Patcharin Cheapchandej and Pakistan's Mahin Aftab Qureshi in the second round.

Eala won bronze medals in women's singles and mixed doubles at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and chose to represent the Philippines in this year's Games despite the tournament's overlap with the WTA calendar.

Obiena, meanwhile, is set to defend his Asian Games men's pole vault title. He won gold in the event at the 2022 Hangzhou Games and is among the Philippine delegation's leading medal prospects in Aichi-Nagoya.
The Philippines sent more than 400 athletes to the 2026 Asian Games, with the country seeking to surpass its four-gold haul from the 2022 edition. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Belfast court injuncts decision to allow Orange Order march down Garvaghy Road
articles.summary: Andy Burnham calls for calm as fears of unrest grow after request for countermarch in mainly nationalist area A controversial loyalist parade down a nationalist street in Portadown has been…

blocks.text: A controversial loyalist parade down a nationalist street in Portadown has been temporarily injuncted after a high court judge urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”.
The ruling was made amid rising fears that a parade could unleash fresh sectarian violence.

After a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court, Justice Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, which was due to take place at 8am on Sunday, until a judicial review application can be fully heard.
She has also suspended the determination by the Parades Commission on Friday that the event could take place, albeit with restrictions on numbers.
However tensions remain with an appeal against her decision by loyalists to be heard at a second special hearing on Saturday night.
Smyth arrived at her conclusions after several attempts to coax the parties, the Loyalist Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, to reach a voluntary agreement.

After it was clear that was not possible, she said: “The level of mistrust between residents and Portadown Loyalist Lodge cannot be overstated. Neither side accepts any of the reassurances of the other.”
The march down Garvaghy Road has been banned for 28 years due to widespread sectarian violence in 1998 outside Drumcree church.
“It is also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland,” she said.
The court was sitting on Saturday following a last-minute legal challenge by the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.
Smyth urged parties to reach a voluntary agreement to delay the march, given few had time to digest the reasoning behind the Commission’s decision.
It was important “to reach an agreement for the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland, not just for your sake” to have the issues “properly aired” so that “everybody knows they’ve had a fair hearing”.
“Be big enough to step back from the abyss,” she told the parties in court.
This followed a high court ruling quashing the restrictions of the annual parade route.

blocks.caption: People gathered outside Belfast high court on Saturday 26 September awaiting the decision by Justice Smyth over the planned Garvaghy Road march. Photograph: Mark Marlow/PA

blocks.text: The Portadown loyalist Orange Lodge was not represented at the hearing. But after a request from the judge for its view through the individual who had sought permission for the parade, the lodge made it clear it would not agree to suspending the procession.

Fears of clashes increased on Saturday after a request to the Commission for permission for a countermarch, a protest that, it was estimated, could be attended by up to 5,000 people, the court heard. That was later revised to 300.

On Friday night, the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, appealed to leaders to “work calmly” through the weekend while the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, called for “cool heads”, saying Northern Ireland had “withstood many moments of sharp disagreement over the years” and must do so again.

Before her ruling, Smyth asked the parties in court, including the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) and the Parades Commission, to “consider carefully the very important issues to our society” raised in this case, and the importance that they were dealt with properly given the “importance of this case to community relations”.
She also noted that the issues of judicial review were of “such fundamental importance” that it could be unwise to hold a full hearing without all the facts.

Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart insisted nationalist residents on the road had “nothing to fear” from the march on Sunday, but Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the decision as “utterly reckless”.

The Parades Commission has placed a number of restrictions on the procession, including an 8am start and limiting the number of participants to 35 people, but not placing any restrictions on the route.

articles.title: Nor'easter storm brings coastal flooding, as New York and New Jersey declare emergency
articles.summary: Tens of millions of people from Maine to Virginia are in the path of the powerful storm.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded

Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm this weekend, which has already brought coastal flooding, power outages, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.

Peaking on Saturday, the so-called nor'easter will "bring dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds, and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, the latter of which is already facing a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
The nor'easter is already causing widespread power outages. Nearly 150,000 households have so far lost electricity, according to poweroutageus.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended flyers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 1,100 flights have been delayed and another 400 grounded, according to FlightAware.
Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal inundations. Streets and homes were flooded on Saturday in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan.
"I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert, and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flooding in New Jersey

blocks.text: Flooding in New Jersey

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flights have been cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport

blocks.text: Flights have been cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport
NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power outages.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs from Sunday afternoon game to next Friday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Waves pound the coast in Massachusetts

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Waves pound the coast in Massachusetts
A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.
Nor is the Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, going ahead.
Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston-area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.
